messages.subject: Adaptation length using rjags
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

Out of curiosity, I would like to know what others, who use rjags, think about how long to run the adaptation phase prior to collecting burn-in samples.  I would guess the correct answer may be "it depends"; as in the specific model structure and data certainly influence the sampler structure (e.g., various combinations of Gibbs and M-H) constructed by JAGS and, thus, how long it takes the adaptation phase to achieve efficiency.

Cheers
Jared

messages.subject: Black box error: Illegal Memory Writing
messages.subject_clean: Black box error: Illegal Memory Writing
messages.body_plain:
Hi all

Did anyone ever have encounter a similar error message?

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-ruSPhuySD-k/V6S35AyufvI/AAAAAAAAQaM/l_rishVbkNAB_3-e6R2wLvao_yfeIDeJgCLcB/s1600/Black_box_error.jpg>

>From what I've read this relates with a memory limit built within WinBUGS and OpenBUGS.

I'm trying to run a multi-species occupancy model for 12 species of fish in 189 sites within a river basin. I want to extrapolate the model for all the basin (~2000 sites).

I'm able to run the model for a few iterations (200) but gives the error message for 2000.

I'm using WinBUGS because my model has an auto regression component and JAGS doesn't allow direct cycles. A model without the spatial component runs well in JAGS but still fails in WinBUGS. So I think it's not a code error, but if you think it can help, I'll upload the code.

Did anyone found such error and was able to circumvent this situation?

Cheers
Mário

I have had this same issue and error message before and was unable to find a work around in WinBUGS. The only reference I could find online about the error was about the built-in memory limits, as well. I, however, was able to run the model as written in JAGS.

I know this doesn't help you get to a solution/work around, but I thought it might give you some sort of confirmation about it likely not being a code issue.

Kelly

messages.subject: PhD oppotunity: Multi-species hierarchical models
messages.body_plain:
Multi-species hierarchical models: developing a better understanding of study design and model performance

Where:  University of Massachusetts-Amherst
When:  January start (but flexible)
Supervisors:
> Chris Sutherland (UMass-Amherst)
> Simone Tenan (MUSE – Museo delle Scienze di Trento)
Applications due:  11 Sept 2016

Project description

The increasing use of the rapidly developing technology available to ecologists, wildlife professionals, and members of the public has made wildlife monitoring an accessible and widely applied practice. The great benefit of methods such as camera traps and/or hair snares is that, despite studies typically being designed with a single species of interest in mind, usually a species of conservation or management concern, they simultaneously detect multiple species that exist on the landscape. Indeed, the single-species approach to tackling ecological, conservation and management issues may not be a sustainable model given the global biodiversity crisis.

In response to an increasing shift towards a multi-species perspective of ecological systems, this PhD will broadly examine for following issues related to two popular classes of hierarchical models – occupancy models, and spatial capture-recapture models:
How reliable are inferences about ‘monitoring by-catch’ species using studies designed for a single species?
What is the optimal multi-species study design that balances the trade-off between achieving inference objectives on priority species and understanding the wider community?

Qualifications

We are looking for applicants that have an interest in both applied and quantitative ecology. There will be a strong quantitative component, so either demonstrable experience or a genuine interest in quantitative ecology is preferable. The candidate should hold a master degree ecology, wildlife biology, natural resources, statistics or a closely related field and would have a minimum experience in R. Candidates would also benefit from having a familiarity with BUGS and hierarchical models (single species or community models). We note, however, that a genuine interest in quantitative ecology goes a long way!

If you are interested in the position, or have any questions, please contact Chris (csuth...@umass.edu) or Simone (simone...@muse.it). To apply, please send a cover letter and detailed CV (as a single document) to Chris (csuth...@umass.edu)

messages.subject: goodenss of fit
messages.body_plain:
Hello dear all, I have some question about GOF. I am reading Kery and Royle book on HIrarchical modeling in ecology. In chapter 8, related to the HDS models the authors said: "The bootstrap analysis shows that the model does not fit at all, with not a single bootstrap sample falling to the right of the observed value, for any of the three fit statistics. That is, under the Null hypothesis of a fitting model, we don’t expect to see any more extreme values of the fit statistics than their value for the observed data set..."

So what I need to do is to accept the null hipotesis that says: the model explains your abundance and detection. Is this correct?

Thank you very much in advance
Antonela
